title: Should Christians Use Images of Jesus? The Question That Becomes More Serious the Longer You Look at Him
paragraphs: Should Christians Use Images of Jesus? The Question That Becomes More Serious the Longer You Look at Him

Before you delete the picture, defend the painting, kiss the icon, condemn the icon, share the AI-generated Jesus, or accuse another Christian of idolatry… there is one question Scripture forces us to ask first: What exactly are we doing with the image—and what has happened inside our hearts?
There is a picture of Jesus on the wall.
Maybe you grew up with one.
Long hair. Gentle eyes. A carefully trimmed beard. Light falling across His face as though heaven itself had paused for the portrait.
Perhaps your grandmother had one hanging above the dining table.
Perhaps there was one in your childhood church.
Maybe you have a picture of Christ carrying a lamb, praying in Gethsemane, standing beside a frightened child, or stretching His wounded hands toward the world.
And maybe looking at it has never bothered you.
Until someone told you:
“That is idolatry.”
Suddenly something that once seemed innocent feels dangerous.
Then another Christian responds:
“No. Jesus became a real human being. Christians have portrayed Him for centuries.”
Now you are caught between two people who both quote Scripture, both confess Christ, and both seem absolutely convinced that the other side is missing something obvious.
So what should a Christian actually believe?
Should Christians use images of Jesus?
Before answering, we need enough humility to admit something important.
The Bible never gives us a verse that simply says, “You may paint Jesus,” or, “You may never draw Jesus.”
That means we must resist the temptation to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But Scripture does give us powerful principles.
And once those principles are placed beside one another, this question becomes far deeper than whether a painting belongs on your wall.
Because this is ultimately a question about worship.
About conscience.
About incarnation.
About idolatry.
And about whether our hearts are satisfied with the Jesus God has revealed—or whether we quietly begin creating a Jesus of our own imagination.
Go back to Sinai.
Smoke.
Fire.
Thunder.
A trembling mountain.
And the voice of God.
Then comes the command:
“לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל”
Lo-ta'aseh lekha pesel.
“You shall not make for yourself a carved image…”
Exodus 20:4 continues by prohibiting the making of a likeness for the purpose described immediately afterward: bowing down to them and serving them.
That context matters.

God was not giving Israel a universal prohibition against every piece of representational artwork. We know this because God Himself later commanded artistic representations to be made in connection with the tabernacle, including cherubim.
The problem was not simply that human hands could produce art.
The horror was that human beings could take something created, fashioned, carved, painted, or imagined and give it the devotion belonging to the Creator.
That distinction matters enormously.
Yet Deuteronomy adds another warning that should make every Christian slow down before dismissing concerns about religious imagery.
Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb:
“You saw no form…”
The Hebrew idea is striking.
Israel heard God.
But they were not given a visible form of God to reproduce.

Therefore Moses warns them against corrupting themselves by making an image in the likeness of male or female. Deuteronomy 4:15–16 connects their not seeing a form with the danger of manufacturing one for themselves.
God would not allow Israel to domesticate Him.
They could not shrink the invisible Creator into something their hands could control.
They could not say:
“This is what God looks like.”
And perhaps that is where this conversation first reaches into us.
Because human beings have always wanted a God we can manage.
A God we can carry.
A God we can decorate.
A God who agrees with us.
A God who never contradicts us.
A God whose face looks exactly as we imagine it should.
But the living God refuses to become the product of human imagination.
Paul makes essentially that point centuries later in Athens.
Surrounded by idols, he declares that the divine nature should not be thought of as gold, silver, or stone—
“χαράγματι τέχνης καὶ ἐνθυμήσεως ἀνθρώπου”
—something fashioned by human art and imagination.
And then Paul moves directly toward repentance.
That warning should never be trivialized.
No painting contains God.
No statue contains God.
No crucifix contains God.
No icon contains God.
No photograph-like reconstruction contains God.
No AI-generated portrait contains God.
And no artist knows the precise facial appearance of Jesus of Nazareth.
Whatever image you have seen is an artistic representation.
It is not a photograph.
It is not an eyewitness portrait supplied by Scripture.
It is not Jesus Himself.
But then Christianity makes an astonishing claim that prevents this discussion from ending there.
Something happened in Bethlehem that had never happened at Sinai.
John writes:
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh…”
John 1:14.
Read those words slowly.
The Word became flesh.
Christianity does not teach that God merely projected a human illusion.
Jesus Christ truly entered human history.
He had a human body.
Human hands.
Human eyes.
Human skin.
People saw Him.
People touched Him.
People ate with Him.
Children could be brought to Him.
John could recline near Him.
Thomas could be invited to see His wounds.
Roman soldiers could seize Him.
A crown of thorns could be pressed onto His head.
Nails could pierce His flesh.
His body could be placed inside a tomb.
And that body could rise.
This is why Christians who permit images of Jesus make an argument that deserves to be represented fairly rather than caricatured.
Their reasoning is not necessarily:
“The Second Commandment does not matter.”
Often their reasoning is exactly the opposite.
They believe the incarnation matters so profoundly that the Son of God truly became visible humanity.
Christ is not merely an invisible spiritual idea.
Paul even calls Jesus:
“εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου”
eikōn tou Theou tou aoratou.
“The image of the invisible God.”
Colossians 1:15.
But we must be extraordinarily careful here.
Paul is describing Christ Himself as the image of the invisible God.
He is not saying that our painting of Christ becomes the image of God in the same sense.
Jesus is unique.
The canvas is not Jesus.
The statue is not Jesus.
The digital illustration is not Jesus.
The icon is not Jesus.
Christ is the incarnate Son.
The artwork is the work of a human being attempting to portray Him.
Confusing those categories is where spiritual danger begins.
Imagine a woman sitting alone late at night.
Her marriage is collapsing.
Her son will not speak to her.
She has prayed until she does not know what else to say.
Across the room hangs a painting of Jesus reaching toward Peter as he sinks beneath the water.
She looks at it.
And suddenly remembers:
“Lord, save me.”
She begins crying.
Not because she believes the canvas can hear her.
Not because she believes paint has supernatural power.
The image simply reminded her of a biblical truth:
Peter sank.
Peter cried out.
Christ rescued him.
Her heart moves beyond the painting to the Savior.
Is that automatically the worship of an idol?
We should be careful before saying yes.
Now change the scene.
Another person stands before an image.
He begins believing the physical object possesses spiritual power.
He trusts the object to protect his house.
He treats touching it as though touching the material object itself guarantees divine favor.
His confidence gradually moves from Christ toward the object.
The representation has become spiritually confused with the One represented.
Now we have entered very dangerous territory.
Because idolatry does not become acceptable simply because the idol has been given a Christian name.
You can write “Jesus” underneath an object and still misuse it.
You can place a cross around your neck and live as though you hate the One who died upon it.
You can own twenty Bibles and refuse to obey a single page.
You can fill your house with Christian artwork while Christ remains unwelcome in your decisions.
And you can have absolutely no religious artwork anywhere in your home while worshiping money, reputation, sexuality, political power, success, comfort, or yourself.
That is the twist we sometimes miss.
A person can remove every picture of Jesus from the house…
and still have a house full of idols.
Because idolatry ultimately reaches deeper than furniture and decoration.
It reaches the throne of the heart.
Yet that does not make physical idolatry imaginary or harmless.
Scripture repeatedly warns God's people against giving created things the worship, trust, devotion, or glory belonging to God.
So perhaps the more revealing question is not merely:
“Do you have an image of Jesus?”
Perhaps it is:
“What are you doing with it?”
Do you believe it is Jesus?
Do you attribute spiritual power to the object itself?
Does your devotion depend upon possessing or touching it?
Has an imagined face begun replacing Scripture's revelation of Christ in your mind?
Are you defending the object more passionately than you defend the Gospel?
Would losing the image feel like losing Jesus?
Those questions matter.
But there is another side.
If you reject images of Jesus, ask yourself something equally uncomfortable.
Do you believe Christians who use them are automatically idolaters even when they explicitly deny worshiping the object?
Have you turned your conviction into a weapon against brothers and sisters?
Have you begun measuring someone's faithfulness to Christ by a disputed application that Scripture does not address in one simple sentence?
Can you distinguish between someone illustrating a biblical event and someone worshiping an object?
Can you disagree without condemning someone's heart when you cannot see that heart?
Romans 14 was not written specifically about religious artwork. Its immediate disputes concerned matters such as food and days, so we should not pretend otherwise.
But Paul's principles concerning conscience, judgment, faith, and stumbling fellow believers are relevant when Christians navigate disputed practices.
He writes:
“Therefore let us not judge one another anymore…”
and urges believers not to place a proskomma or skandalon—a stumbling block or occasion for falling—in another believer's path.
Later comes an even more sobering principle:
“πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν.”
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”
Romans 14:23.
That should stop both sides from behaving carelessly.
If your conscience, informed by Scripture, will not allow you to use an image of Jesus in good faith before God, do not violate your conscience merely because someone calls you legalistic.
You do not need the picture.
You need Christ.

But if another believer uses a biblical illustration as art, education, storytelling, historical imagination, or a reminder of a Gospel event without worshiping it, do not casually pronounce a judgment on that person's soul that Scripture itself has not explicitly pronounced.
And if you do use images of Jesus, hold them loosely.
Very loosely.
Never confuse imagination with revelation.
Never pretend we know Jesus' precise earthly appearance when Scripture does not give us a portrait.
Never allow an artist's face of Jesus to become more authoritative in your imagination than Scripture's revelation of Jesus.
Because Scripture gives us something infinitely better than a reconstruction of His cheekbones.
It tells us who He is.
Holy.
Merciful.
Righteous.
Compassionate.
Sinless.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
King.
Savior.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The image of the invisible God.
The One through whom and for whom all things were created.
The One before whom every knee will bow.
That is the Jesus we cannot afford to replace.
And perhaps this is where the argument suddenly stops being about somebody else's wall.
Because there is a far more dangerous image of Jesus than anything hanging inside a church.
It is the Jesus we manufacture inside ourselves.
The Jesus who never confronts our sin.
The Jesus who approves every desire.
The Jesus who exists to make us wealthy.
The Jesus who hates everyone we hate.
The Jesus who belongs to our political tribe.
The Jesus who never says, “Repent.”
The Jesus who gives heaven without lordship, forgiveness without repentance, Christianity without a cross, and grace without transformation.
That Jesus may never be painted.
He may never be carved.
He may never hang on a wall.
But he can still be an idol.
And perhaps some of us have spent years arguing about pictures of Jesus while worshiping a Jesus created in the image of ourselves.
That should frighten us more.
Because the Gospel does not invite us to invent Christ.
It calls us to surrender to Him.
The real Jesus does not exist to decorate our lives.
He comes to save sinners.
He comes to expose darkness.
He comes with grace for the ashamed and truth for the self-deceived.
He touches lepers.
He receives the broken.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes repentant sinners.
He carries a cross.
And then, astonishingly, He carries our sin upon it.
Maybe that is why this question becomes so emotional.
Somewhere beneath the theological arguments is a human heart desperately wanting to see Jesus.
We want something tangible.
Something close.
Something we can look at when life becomes unbearable.
But Christian hope goes beyond every painting ever made.
One day faith will become sight.
Not because an artist finally produces the perfect portrait.
Not because artificial intelligence reconstructs the right face.
Not because archaeologists discover the right image.
But because Christ Himself will be seen.
Until then, Scripture calls us to know Him through the revelation God has actually given us and to worship Him in spirit and truth.
So should Christians use images of Jesus?

Scripture gives clear prohibitions against idolatry and against reducing the divine nature to the products of human art and imagination. It also gives us the astonishing reality that the eternal Son truly became flesh and was genuinely seen by human beings. What Scripture does not give us is a simple verse explicitly settling every modern use of a visual depiction of Jesus.
Therefore, Christians should approach the question with biblical conviction, humility, and a guarded conscience.
Never worship an image.
Never trust an image.
Never attribute divine power to an image.
Never confuse an artistic representation with Christ Himself.
Never allow an imagined face to replace the biblical Christ.
Never violate your conscience simply to fit in.
And never make your own conclusion on a disputed application an excuse for pride, contempt, or careless judgment toward another believer.
If an image leads you toward superstition, misplaced devotion, confusion, or violation of conscience, remove it.
Christ is infinitely more precious than the object.
If you use an image simply as illustration or art, remember every time you see it:
This is not His photograph.
This is not His presence.
This is not my mediator.
This cannot hear me.
This cannot save me.
Jesus Christ can.
And perhaps someone reading this has discovered something more painful than a theological disagreement.
Maybe you realized you have been carrying a counterfeit Jesus.
Not necessarily in your hands.
In your heart.
A convenient Jesus.
A manageable Jesus.
A Jesus who never gets close enough to touch the secret you have protected for years.
But the living Christ already knows.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness hidden behind Christian vocabulary.
The affair nobody discovered.
The resentment toward God.
The prayer life that disappeared months ago.
The church smile covering spiritual exhaustion.
The addiction.
The pride.
The secret unbelief.
The shame.
The thing you keep promising Jesus you will stop doing.
He knows.
And still the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful.
Christ died for sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not impressive sinners.
Sinners.
At the cross, the Holy One took the judgment His people deserved.
And the risen Christ still calls sinners to repent, believe, come into the light, and receive mercy.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by telling you darkness is actually light.
Grace does something far more glorious.
Grace meets the guilty person at the place where excuses finally die…
and offers forgiveness purchased by Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to perform for us.
But you can be honest.

And if you disagree about images of Jesus, let the comments demonstrate something the world rarely sees anymore: Christians capable of conviction without cruelty. Tell us what Scripture has persuaded you to believe and why. Then listen to another believer before assuming the worst about them.
Not because every sentence must become your conclusion, but because these Scriptures deserve more than a five-second reaction.
Send it to the person who once asked you whether Christian images are idols and you did not know how to answer.
It does not.
Not because giving can purchase salvation.
It cannot.
Christian generosity must never be manipulated.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be a genuine voluntary expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and for the glory of God.
And sometimes supporting Gospel work costs less than we imagine.
One shared article.
One friend tagged.
One believer deciding that instead of merely consuming Christian content, they will help useful biblical content reach somebody else.

If you want to glorify God through your resources, there are many faithful ways to do that: care for your family, serve your local church, help the poor, support missions and Gospel ministry, practice hospitality, and give generously as God enables you. Supporting Gospel Warrior can be one voluntary part of that larger life of Christian generosity.
Free resources because truth should reach people who cannot afford another purchase.
And the Gospel at the center because none of this matters if people remember Gospel Warrior but forget Jesus.
But above everything else…
Follow Christ.
Because when the paintings fade, when the screens go dark, when our arguments are forgotten, when every earthly ministry has finished its assignment, there will still be Jesus.
Not an artist's Jesus.
Not your imagined Jesus.
Not my preferred Jesus.
Not a Jesus reconstructed to fit the culture.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
And coming again.
So whether there is a picture of Jesus hanging on your wall or you would never permit one inside your home, make certain there is no rival sitting on the throne that belongs to Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be getting the painting wrong.
It would be spending your life defending an image of Jesus while never surrendering to Jesus Himself.
